responseText: {"galleries":[{"id":"nifty-faces--locked-geometry","title":"Faces Built from Boxes","question":"What can a face built entirely from rectangles show that a drawn face cannot?","introduction":"Every face here is constructed from stacked and nested rectangles — eye boxes, tooth bars, brow bands — rather than drawn as a continuous form. Moving through seventeen works, the exhibition traces how that rigid geometry is established, loaded with competing marks, and finally pushed to the point where its compartments can no longer hold their contents.","closing":"Rectangles divide a face into zones. By the final works, those zones are labeled, leaking, and visibly strained — which raises the question of what the geometry was doing in the first place.","chapters":[{"title":"The Basic Grammar","introduction":"Three works establish the core structure: a face divided into hard-edged zones, each feature assigned its own rectangular compartment with a distinct interior."},{"title":"Flat Grounds, Direct Address","introduction":"Four works place the rectangular face against a single saturated color, removing spatial depth and pushing the assembled features into unmediated contact with the viewer."},{"title":"Compartments at Capacity","introduction":"Five works fill each rectangular zone with competing marks — crossed lines, spirals, packed strokes — until the interior of every compartment is working against its own boundary."},{"title":"Scaffolding Made Visible","introduction":"Four works pull back from maximum density toward a structural, diagrammatic quality: the face reads as a plan or diagram rather than a presence, and the scaffolding itself becomes the subject."},{"title":"The Frame Under Strain","introduction":"The final two works push the rectangular structure to its limit: marks escape their zones, labels appear on the grid, and the geometry reads as something it can no longer fully organize."}]},{"id":"nifty-faces--radiating-pressure","title":"Lines That Cannot Stay Inside","question":"When marks escape the face's boundary, what remains to hold the face together?","introduction":"Fifteen works share a single observable condition: lines that extend past the face they describe. Some push outward in hard diagonals; others dissolve the boundary until figure and field occupy the same visual register. The exhibition moves from faces where the boundary still holds, through works where the overflow competes equally with the features, to images where the face is readable only through density.","closing":"Where the boundary holds, the face is legible. Where it gives way, the marks continue into the field — and what remains is still, just barely, a face. The question is what is doing the holding.","chapters":[{"title":"The Boundary Holds","introduction":"Four works where a recognizable face dominates the composition, even as lines press against its edges and begin to extend past them into the surrounding field."},{"title":"Overflow as the Main Event","introduction":"Five works where the lines escaping the face are as visually prominent as the face itself — the boundary and the field competing on equal terms for attention."},{"title":"Density Without Outline","introduction":"Three works where the face emerges from accumulated marks rather than drawn edges — features readable only because lines pile up more thickly in some areas than others."},{"title":"The Grid Imposed on the Dissolving Face","introduction":"Three works that place rectangular framing or a structural grid over a face already losing its boundary — testing whether geometry can recover what the overflow has dispersed."}]},{"id":"nifty-faces--mismatched-eyes","title":"Two Eyes, Two Systems","question":"When a face's two eyes are built from different shapes or visual logics, what does the rest of the face do?","introduction":"Every face here carries a visible split: two eye zones built from different shapes, different mark systems, or different visual weights. Some differences are subtle — a slight shift in height or framing. Others are total opposites. Moving through this gallery, notice how that single asymmetry changes what the whole face appears to be doing, and whether a mouth full of teeth settles the question or opens another.","closing":"Fifteen faces, none of them symmetrical. Whether the asymmetry reads as alertness, imbalance, or something else may depend entirely on which eye you look at first.","chapters":[{"title":"Unequal but Contained","introduction":"These faces hold their asymmetry inside a stable overall structure. The two eye zones differ in mark or color, but the form stays composed — the split is present without tipping into disorder."},{"title":"Radiating Against Winding","introduction":"Here the asymmetry becomes structural: one eye expands outward through rings or petals while the other contracts inward through spirals, placing opposite visual logics side by side."},{"title":"Three Eyes and Other Departures","introduction":"Two faces complicate the count itself — one presents three eye-like forms, another reduces one eye to near-absence. The asymmetry is no longer just left versus right."},{"title":"Asymmetry Inside Dense Surfaces","introduction":"These faces carry their asymmetry inside surfaces packed with layered lines and competing marks. The split between the eyes is one visible difference among many."},{"title":"Split to the Edge","introduction":"The final group pushes asymmetry toward its limit: faces where competing mark systems or a single overwhelming feature make the two sides feel like separate compositions sharing one outline."}]},{"id":"nifty-faces--silhouette-and-shadow","title":"Dark Mass, Small Light","question":"How little light does a face need to remain a face?","introduction":"Sixteen works each test the same question from a different position. Some faces are still largely readable, their surfaces layered but their features present. Others retreat behind dark washes, dense mark-making, or near-total blackness, holding on by a single bright accent — a yellow bar, a tooth row, a blue iris. The exhibition traces that gradual withdrawal and asks where recognition ends.","closing":"By the final works, the question is no longer whether a face is present but whether the small remaining light is enough to hold it together — and what kind of light counts.","chapters":[{"title":"Surface and Presence","introduction":"Four faces where the form is still largely readable, but the surface already resists easy description — layered with marks or tonal depth that complicate what lies beneath."},{"title":"Line Against Dark","introduction":"Four works where darkness has claimed most of the surface and drawn lines — rather than tonal gradation — carry the work of keeping a face present."},{"title":"Buried Under Marks","introduction":"Three works where the face is covered by dense, competing mark-making. The question of recognition shifts from shadow to sheer visual accumulation."},{"title":"Skull Logic","introduction":"Three works that strip the face back to its most reduced vocabulary — sockets, teeth, and outline — testing how little structural information recognition actually requires."},{"title":"The Last Light","introduction":"Two works where darkness has absorbed most of the form and a single small accent — yellow bars, white marks — is all that remains to locate the face."}]},{"id":"nifty-faces--bared-teeth","title":"Teeth Showing","question":"What does the surrounding surface do to a mouth that is already open?","introduction":"Twenty-five faces, each with teeth showing. Some sit against flat saturated grounds that push them forward; others dissolve into scribble or shadow. The exhibition follows the tooth-filled mouth from its most readable forms — where a first response is still available — through works where the marks covering the face pull so hard against the opening that no single reading holds.","closing":"Each face here shows its teeth. Whether that reads as greeting, warning, or something with no ready name depends on marks the works themselves leave unresolved.","chapters":[{"title":"A Legible First Reading","introduction":"Four faces where the open mouth and its surroundings still allow a recognizable first response — before the surrounding marks begin to complicate it."},{"title":"Flat Grounds, Emblem Faces","introduction":"Six works where a saturated, unmodulated background removes spatial depth, turning the face into something closer to a sign or emblem than a portrait."},{"title":"Surface Working Against the Mouth","introduction":"Six faces where the marks covering the skin create a visual argument of their own — the tooth-filled mouth competes with a surface that appears to be doing something else."},{"title":"Volume and Shadow","introduction":"Five faces that use modeled light and shadow rather than flat grounds, giving the teeth a different kind of weight — embedded in mass rather than announced against color."},{"title":"The Expression That Will Not Settle","introduction":"Four faces where the open mouth and the surrounding marks pull in opposite directions, leaving the expression without a stable reading."}]},{"id":"nifty-faces--objects-letters-emblems","title":"When the Face Carries Signs","question":"What can a face still communicate once its features have been replaced, interrupted, or overwritten by marks and objects?","introduction":"These twenty-five works share a single territory: the human face as a surface where marks, symbols, and objects compete with portraiture. Some faces carry their signs lightly; others are nearly consumed by them. Moving from crossed eyes and barred mouths through gridded diagrams and split color fields, the exhibition traces how far a sign can advance into a face before the portrait disappears.","closing":"Each work leaves the question open differently. Whether a sign cancels a feature or simply joins it, something shifts in what the face can hold and what it can no longer show.","chapters":[{"title":"The X and the Eye","introduction":"Four faces where a single repeated mark — the X or cross — lands directly on the eyes, converting the gaze into a sign of blockage or negation."},{"title":"Objects in Place of Features","introduction":"Works where a discrete object — a hand, a heart, glasses — occupies the position of a facial feature, displacing rather than decorating it."},{"title":"Marks That Contest the Portrait","introduction":"Faces where geometric signs, scribbled lines, or color divisions actively compete with the portrait for visual authority — neither fully winning."},{"title":"Letters, Numbers, and Diagrams","introduction":"Works where legible text, repeated symbols, or diagrammatic layouts enter the face, making the image readable as both portrait and notation simultaneously."},{"title":"The Face Reduced to Structure","introduction":"Five works where the sign system has advanced so far that the face is present only in placement or outline — the features no longer dominant, the signs no longer decorative."}]},{"id":"nifty-faces--accumulation-and-dissolution","title":"Faces Made of Layers","question":"At what point does the accumulation of marks stop describing a face and become its own subject?","introduction":"These twenty-one works share a single subject — the human face — but treat it as a site where marks multiply, compete, and sometimes overwhelm what they describe. Moving from portraits where features hold their ground through works where mark systems run on their own logic, the exhibition asks how much a face can absorb before the marks become the primary event.","closing":"Each work here began with a face. Whether it still ends with one — or with something the marks have replaced — is a question each visitor will reach at a different point.","chapters":[{"title":"The Face Holds","introduction":"Three works where recognizable features — eyes, nose, mouth — remain legible despite visible layering. The marks are present but the face is still the dominant reading."},{"title":"Structure Under Strain","introduction":"Works where the face is still present but its features have been reorganized into competing systems — spirals, grids, slashes — each running on its own visual logic."},{"title":"The Face as Architecture","introduction":"Works where the face has been reorganized into stacked chambers, rectangular zones, or structural grids — still a face, but one that reads as built rather than drawn."},{"title":"Marks Competing for the Same Space","introduction":"Works where multiple mark systems — hatching, loops, spirals, slashes — press against each other until the face becomes a site of collision rather than a stable description."},{"title":"When the Marks Take Over","introduction":"Works where the face is nominally present but the marks have become the primary event — features reduced to fixed points inside a field that operates on its own terms."}]}]}
